verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and message #2 itself asks for agreement on the on-disk representation before code review. That agreement needs evidence for the workloads the commit message names (demand-1), a check that skip keys cover their groups (maintenance-fit-1), and an answer on the Penalty assumption (maintenance-fit-2). Nobody but the author has posted, so the design is not yet discussed.

brief.title: GiST skip tuples for page-local grouping on internal pages
brief.problem: Scanning a GiST internal page applies the consistent function to every downlink, and insertion computes penalty for every downlink. This costs most for operator classes with expensive keys and for pages with high fanout. The author also expects it to protect GiST from slowdown on large block sizes.
brief.proposed_design: Internal pages carry skip tuples, each holding the union key of the downlinks that follow it, so scans and subtree selection can reject a whole group at once. A skip tuple is marked by InvalidBlockNumber in t_tid, with the group size in ip_posid. Skip tuples are derived metadata kept up to date by inserts, splits, both build methods and VACUUM, and existing WAL records log full page states.
user_visible_surface: On-disk GiST internal page format gains skip tuples; existing pages need no conversion, per the author.
author_claims: On 5M uniform points with point_ops, all data in cache, a join runs 1.41x faster, point queries 1.13x, and inserts 1.12x.
Index size grows by about 0.05%, and 0.2% on a larger index.
Build time shows no measurable difference, because master varies by 27% run to run on the test machine.
Operator classes with a more expensive Consistent should gain more; the author has not tested this.
The format does not use INDEX_AM_RESERVED_BIT and needs no new WAL record type or pg_upgrade step.
brief.thread_state: Only the author has posted: a 2018 first version and a 2026 revival with v3. He asks for opinions on the on-disk representation before code review, and CFbot reports the patch needs a rebase.
unclear: The material does not say how older binaries or tools such as amcheck and pageinspect treat pages that contain skip tuples, for example after a downgrade.
No numbers cover data larger than shared_buffers, other operator classes, multi-column indexes or non-default block sizes.
The group size is fixed at 16 and untuned, and the material gives no way to choose it.
The material does not say whether concurrent scans stay correct while VACUUM or an insert rebuilds a group.
The material does not explain why the 2018 and 2026 results differ beyond possible measurement error.

objections.title: The motivating workloads are not measured
objections.failure_scenario: A committer accepts a permanent change to the GiST internal page format on the strength of point_ops with all data in cache. Later, users of costly operator classes or non-default block sizes, the cases the proposal names, see little or no gain. The project still carries the format and its maintenance cost in inserts, splits, both builds and VACUUM.
objections.argument: The commit message justifies the change by operator classes with costly keys and by high fanout, and message #1 adds large block sizes. Message #2 measures neither and says the costly-Consistent gain "is untested". The only numbers cover one cheap operator class, in cache, with a gain of about 1.13x on point queries and 1.12x on inserts. The 2018 numbers in message #1 showed a different balance, and message #2 attributes the gap to measurement error, so the size of the gain for real users is not yet shown.
objections.author_must_show: For which widely used operator classes or block sizes does Consistent or Penalty cost dominate GiST time, and what speedup does v3 give there with data larger than shared_buffers?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 says the costly-Consistent case is untested, and no numbers cover large block sizes or data larger than shared_buffers. Saying so in the thread does not supply the evidence for the workloads the commit message names.

objections.title: Union key coverage must hold on every internal-page update path
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a new path that changes an internal page, such as a new page-deletion step or a parent-key adjustment, and does not rebuild the group union. A scan then rejects a group whose skip key no longer covers a downlink, and queries silently miss rows until someone runs a full comparison against a seqscan.
objections.argument: The README hunk makes correctness depend on every page update rebuilding the affected group, but the patch adds no check for that. Today a stale or missing downlink key is the only way GiST loses rows. The patch adds a second key layer whose staleness has the same effect. The touched files do not include amcheck, so nothing would verify that a skip key covers its group.
objections.author_must_show: Will amcheck verify that each skip key covers its group, so a future path that forgets the rebuild fails a check before it returns wrong results?

critic.reasoning: The README makes scan correctness depend on every internal-page update rebuilding the group key. The TAP test covers today's paths only, and the material names no check that would catch a later path that omits the rebuild.

objections.title: Subtree skipping assumes a penalty property opclasses do not promise
objections.failure_scenario: A group's union is a wide, flat box, and a new point lies just above the middle of it. The enlargement penalty for the union is large, while one small member box needs almost no enlargement, so insertion skips the best subtree. Tree quality then degrades over time, and nobody connects later slow scans to this skipping rule.
objections.argument: Message #1 states the rule assumes an enlarged key never has a higher penalty than its members. Area-enlargement penalties, which point_ops uses, do not guarantee this, and third-party opclasses were written without that contract. The insert benchmark in message #2 measures speed only, not the tree quality produced over many inserts.
objections.author_must_show: Which penalty functions satisfy the monotonicity assumption, and how does tree quality after many inserts compare with master for box and point opclasses?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 states the assumption, and area-enlargement penalties do not guarantee it when the new key lies outside a wide union. Only index quality is affected, and the uniform-point benchmark would not show it, so it stays fixable.

objections.title: Page inspection tools will report skip tuples as ordinary downlinks
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA runs pageinspect's gist_page_items on an internal page. It lists entries with an invalid block number and a small offset next to real downlinks. External tools that walk GiST pages count these entries as children or report the page as corrupt.
objections.argument: The patch's touched-files list covers only access/gist and a new test module, not contrib/pageinspect or contrib/amcheck. The new marker reuses t_tid fields that existing readers treat as a downlink. Message #2 asks for opinions on exactly this on-disk representation, so the readers it affects belong in that discussion.
objections.author_must_show: How will pageinspect, any GiST checking in amcheck, and third-party page readers identify skip tuples and show or verify them?

critic.reasoning: The touched-files list has nothing under contrib, and pageinspect's gist_page_items reads internal tuples today. Message #2 asks for opinions on this representation, so how readers outside access/gist identify skip tuples is a fair question.

objections.title: Group rebuild adds Union calls to every internal-page insert
objections.failure_scenario: An application inserts into a GiST index whose opclass has an expensive Union, such as signature-based tsvector or intarray. Each downlink adjustment now also recomputes a group union over up to 16 keys, so insert throughput can drop where the benchmark showed a gain.
objections.argument: The commit message says page updates rebuild the affected group from its real tuples. The only insert numbers use point_ops, where Union is cheap. Message #2 says expensive opclasses should gain on Consistent but does not discuss the matching cost on Union during inserts.
objections.author_must_show: What is the insert cost with an opclass whose Union is expensive, compared with master?

critic.reasoning: The commit message says page updates rebuild the affected group from its real tuples. The only insert numbers use point_ops, so the cost with an expensive Union is not shown.

refuted.title: Insert-time group skipping assumes a penalty property opclasses never promised
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension opclass uses an enlargement-style Penalty, as box and point do. A new point lies just outside a small member box, but the group's union is wide, so the union penalty exceeds the best found so far and the group is skipped. The insert descends into a worse subtree, and the user sees slower queries on that index only after many inserts, with no error.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states the rule: the union key's penalty must be less than or equal to each member's penalty. The GiST opclass contract does not require this, and area enlargement often grows with key size, so the rule can fail even for core opclasses. Message #2 and the README keep the skip rule but no longer state the assumption. The only measurements use uniform points, where reduced index quality would be hard to see.
refuted.author_must_show: Which documented Penalty property makes skipping a group safe for index quality, and do box_ops, btree_gist and common extension opclasses actually satisfy it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2, which gives the more concrete geometric case and also asks for a tree-quality comparison.

refuted.title: Code outside access/gist still assumes every internal tuple is a downlink
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA runs a GiST structure check, or a page-inspection tool, on an index built by the patched server. The tool reads a skip tuple with InvalidBlockNumber as a downlink. It then reports corruption, errors out, or shows a bogus child pointer, and the DBA finds out during an incident check.
refuted.argument: The patch changes what an internal GiST page may hold, but every touched file is in access/gist, gist_private.h or the new test module. Nothing in contrib appears in the list, and nothing says how amcheck, pageinspect or out-of-tree page readers should treat skip tuples. Skip tuples carry no page flag, so a reader can only spot them by the block number, and readers written before the patch never check it. Message #2 asks for opinions on this exact representation, so the readers outside access/gist belong in that discussion.
refuted.author_must_show: Which in-tree and known external readers walk GiST internal pages, how will each recognize skip tuples, and would a page-level flag make detection safer?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. This version also states that skip tuples carry no page flag, which the material does not say.

refuted.title: Permanent on-disk format change rests on one in-cache benchmark
refuted.failure_scenario: The format ships, and later releases find that the fixed group size of 16 or the scheme does not help for larger-than-memory data or other opclasses. Every later release must still read and maintain skip tuples on pages that pg_upgrade carried over, even if the feature stops creating them.
refuted.argument: Message #2 asks reviewers to approve the representation before anything else, yet the evidence is one opclass, uniform points, data fully in shared_buffers, and an untuned group size. The 2018 and 2026 results disagree on where the gain comes from, and message #2 attributes the 2018 result to possible measurement error. A format decision outlives every one of these choices.
refuted.author_must_show: Do the gains hold for data larger than shared_buffers, an expensive opclass such as tsvector or PostGIS geometry, and at least two group sizes?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which states the same evidence gap. The added regret argument is weaker, because the README says removing skip tuples leaves a valid ordinary GiST page.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: GiST internal pages gain skip tuples, marked by InvalidBlockNumber in t_tid with the group size in ip_posid.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Existing GiST WAL records carry page states that now include skip tuples; the test covers standby replay and crash recovery.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Group skipping on insert relies on a Penalty property of operator classes, and page readers outside access/gist see a new tuple kind.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Inserts, splits, both build methods and VACUUM must keep skip tuples correct, and so must every later change to internal pages.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes GiST internal-page scans and subtree choice, and adds a group Union rebuild on page updates.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: The motivating workloads are not measured

questions: What speedup does v3 give for an operator class with an expensive Consistent, with data larger than shared_buffers, and at a non-default block size?
Will amcheck or another check verify that each skip key covers its group, so a later update path that omits the rebuild fails before a scan misses rows?
Which Penalty functions satisfy the assumption from message #1, and how does tree quality after many inserts compare with master for box and point operator classes?
How will pageinspect's gist_page_items, amcheck and third-party page readers identify skip tuples and show or verify them?
What is the insert cost compared with master for an operator class with an expensive Union, and how should the group size of 16 be chosen?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the GiST insert, split, build and VACUUM code and its WAL replay. Only the author has posted in the thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a GiST internal page format that later releases must read for as long as pg_upgrade carries such indexes. A skip key that fails to cover its group makes scans miss rows.
committability.author_follow_up: The author revived the thread in 2026 with v3 and moved the CommitFest entry forward. The rebase that CFbot asked for on 2026-10-12 is not in the thread.

priority.reason: Any GiST user could gain, and point_ops in cache shows 1.12x to 1.41x, but the patch changes the page format and every internal-page update path. The author asked for opinions on the representation and no one has answered.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can judge whether concurrent scans stay correct while an insert or VACUUM rebuilds a group, or whether every internal-page update path rebuilds the group key. How older page readers handle the marker is also unchecked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pageinspect - add functions on GIN and GiST indexes from gevel
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Alexander Korotkov, Tomas Vondra, Ashutosh Sharma, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the gevel module's functions for GiST, SP-GiST and GIN indexes into pageinspect, with tests and docs. The functions show whole-index statistics, print the tree and its stored objects, and estimate GIN value counts and query matches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said the functions read the whole index, while pageinspect inspects single pages, so the code belongs in a new extension or should be rewritten as page-level functions. Peter Eisentraut also found that the patch no longer compiled and that the stats functions returned one formatted text value where they should return a row with columns. The author planned a new contrib module but posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback after three weeks of waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The proposed patch uses a very different approach, reading the whole index,
not individual pages. Why should it be part of pageinspect?

precedents_retrieved.title: Cube extension GiST penalty function improvement
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Greg Stark, Heikki Linnakangas
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the cube extension's GiST penalty function to follow the RR*-tree choose-subtree rules, preferring entries that need no enlargement and using edge sum (margin) for zero-volume cases. It packs several ranked criteria into one float by reinterpreting its IEEE 754 bit pattern, and later versions fall back to the old penalty when __STDC_IEC_559__ is not defined.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane and Greg Stark objected to the float bit-twiddling because project policy does not allow code to assume IEEE 754, and the author himself later called the technique controversial. Heikki Linnakangas then asked why the patch uses edge sums instead of the volume of the non-zero dimensions, and the thread stalled. Michael Paquier marked the patch returned with feedback, and the author said a planned GiST API and cube patch would make this one unnecessary.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This thread has basically died, so marking as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: enum support in btree_gin and btree_gist
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds enum support to the btree_gin and btree_gist extensions, without distance operators and so without KNN support. The enum comparison goes through enum_cmp_internal, which uses the type cache for enums whose values are not in OID order.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Testing showed that GiST comparisons gave wrong results after alter type ... add value, because enum_cmp_internal expects fcinfo->flinfo and DirectFunctionCallN passes NULL. Tom Lane judged a NULL check too slow and said the proper fix is to pass the FunctionCallInfo through the btree_gist/gin intermediate layer, which touches almost every function. The author agreed but had no time to do this before the end of the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The problem is that the intermediate layer in btree_gist (and
probably btree_gin too, didn't look) does not pass through the
FunctionCallInfo data structure that's provided by the GIST AM.

precedents_retrieved.title: support for box type in SP-GiST index
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds an SP-GiST operator class for the box type that treats a 2D box as a point in 4D space and indexes it with a quad-tree analogue (q4d) splitting each node into 16 regions. It also adds a traversalValue field to SP-GiST so inner_consistent can carry computed bounds to child nodes, and switches range_spgist.c from reconstructValue to it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers asked for performance numbers, a fuller explanation of the patch's purpose, and a rebase, and the patch was set to Waiting on Author. The author did not reply, so it was closed after about three months without a response.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I closed this patch as "returned with feedback" because the author
didn't reply in three months.

precedents_retrieved.title: Better tracking of free space during SP-GiST index build
precedents_retrieved.summary: Tom Lane proposed that SP-GiST index build track several recently used pages per page category instead of only the last one, so that free space is reused better. A fixed table gives more cache slots to leaf pages than to other categories.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No one objected to the patch, and Tomas Vondra called it a solid improvement. After review, Tom Lane planned to make page selection by free space more efficient. He did not have time for that before the commitfest ended, so he asked for the entry to be marked returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I doubt I will get to it this week, so let's mark it RWF for this fest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Compress method for SP-GiST
precedents_retrieved.authors: Heikki Linnakangas (heikki), Fedor Sigaev (sigaev), Alexander Korotkov (smagen), Nikita Glukhov (n.glukhov)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an optional compress method to SP-GiST operator classes so that the leaf data type stored in the index can differ from the indexed column type, for example storing a bounding box for a polygon or circle. This requires the SP-GiST code to distinguish the input type from the leaf type (and to handle reconstructed values accordingly), together with opclasses that use it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The final closing message states that reviews of the patches posted earlier in the thread were not answered and that the patch set had conflicts with HEAD and needed a rebase, so the entry was returned with feedback. The later discussion had turned to a separate NaN/infinity bug in bounding-box computation, which was asked to move to its own thread. In earlier commitfests the entry had also been returned with feedback for lack of author response and no new patch version.

The set of
patches also have conflicts with HEAD so they need a rebase. For those
reasons I am marking this entry as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit ee1e5662d8d8330726eaef7d3110cb7add24d058, as well as
a remarkably large number of followup commits, which were mostly concerned
with the fact that the implementation didn't work terribly well.  It still

if we want to fully support GUCs whose default varies depending on the
value of another GUC.  Meanwhile, it also emerged that there wasn't really

effective_cache_size should default to 4 times shared_buffers).  So whack
it all back to where it was.  In a followup commit, I'll do what was
recently agreed to, which is to simply change the default to a higher
value.

precedents_retrieved.title: PageRepairFragmentation optimization
precedents_retrieved.summary: Heikki Linnakangas proposed speeding up PageRepairFragmentation, which profiling of WAL replay showed spending much of its time in qsort of item ids, by replacing the qsort() call with a bucket sort specialised for small arrays of item offsets. The patch came in two parts: a refactoring that moved code shared by PageRepairFragmentation, PageIndexMultiDelete and PageIndexDeleteNoCompact into a common function, and the sort replacement.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The refactoring part was committed after review. For the bucket-sort part, Peter Geoghegan asked about the choice of N_SORT_BUCKETS and why bucket sort was chosen over alternatives such as a specialised quicksort, and later asked for its status. No reply from the author appears after that, so the visible messages show the remaining work stalled without a response rather than being rejected on technical grounds.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in SP-Gist index
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds explicit predicate locking to the SP-GiST index access method for serializable isolation. It takes predicate locks only on leaf pages and copies a lock from the original page to the new page during a page split.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Alexander Korotkov found that locking only leaf pages misses conflicts. When choose returns spgAddNode, the insert adds a new branch that earlier scans could have used, so internal pages need predicate locks too. He also found that the patch moves predicate locks only when doPickSplit() allocates a new leaf page, but SP-GiST can move items to free space on another busy page. Daniel Gustafsson returned the patch based on this review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
And this new branch could probably be used by scans we
made in the past.  Therefore, you need to do predicate locking for internal
pages too in order to detect all the possible conflicts.

This undoes a poorly-thought-out choice in commit 970a18687f9b3058, namely
to export guc.c's internal variable data_directory.  The authoritative
variable so far as C code is concerned is DataDir; there is no reason for

After yesterday's commits fixing the fsync-on-restart patch, the only

This is mostly cosmetic, so no need for a back-patch (and I'd be hesitant
to remove a global variable in stable branches anyway).

precedents_retrieved.objection: Doing I/O to large tables would consume a lot of address space or require frequent mapping/unmapping. precedents_retrieved.summary:
Indeterminate behavior for the GROUP BY clause

precedents_retrieved.objection: At least one other database product allows specification of a subset of the result columns which GROUP BY would need to be able to provide predictable results; the server is free to return any value from the group. precedents_retrieved.title: MONEY dumps in a locale-specific format making it difficult to restore to a system with a different locale
precedents_retrieved.summary:
MONEY dumps in a locale-specific format making it difficult to restore to a system with a different locale
Section: Data Types / MONEY Data Type

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent matches, so no earlier rejection reason applies here. Message #1 points to an earlier proposal to build a small GiST inside each page and reports two design changes since then: two levels instead of many, and a counter instead of a tid so no pg_upgrade is needed. The 2018 version drew no replies, which shows no engagement but records no rejection reason.
There is no SQL, GUC, psql or pg_dump surface. Indexes created on older versions need no conversion, and downgrade across major versions is not supported anyway.

WAL looks sound as described: existing records log full page states, and the test covers standby replay and crash recovery. Old pages need no conversion, and physical standbys must run the same major version anyway, so the only issue left on this angle is readers outside access/gist.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect: it adds no SQL surface, privilege, setting or view. Skip tuples call the same Consistent, Union and Penalty functions the operator class already runs, on keys derived from existing downlinks. Downgrade and tool handling of the new marker are format concerns for other angles.

Postgres has no feature, setting or documented idiom that groups downlinks inside a GiST internal page so Consistent or Penalty can reject a group at once. An extension cannot add this, because the page layout belongs to the GiST access method in core. The sorted build and the buffered build improve index quality but do not cut the number of Consistent calls per page, and an alternative such as SP-GiST is a different index type.
Faster GiST scans and inserts would help any GiST user, so broad demand is plausible. The objection is that the material does not yet show gains for the workloads that motivate the change.
